name: Actinic prurigo
aliases: hereditary polymorphic light eruption of American Indians

clinicalPearls: A persistent, intensely itchy photodermatosis that usually begins in childhood and is especially prevalent in indigenous populations of the Americas, though it is seen worldwide
There is a strong association with HLA-DR4, and in particular the HLA-DRB1*0407 subtype, supporting an inherited susceptibility
Excoriated papules and nodules develop on sun-exposed skin, but unlike polymorphic light eruption the eruption often extends onto covered sites and may persist through winter
Cheilitis, typically of the lower lip, is a highly characteristic and sometimes presenting feature, and conjunctivitis may also occur
The face, particularly the nasal bridge, and the distal limbs are commonly involved, and chronic scratching leads to lichenification and scarring
It tends to be perennial with summer exacerbation, in contrast to the clearly seasonal course of polymorphic light eruption
Management combines rigorous photoprotection with treatment of the itch and inflammation, and phototherapy hardening or systemic agents are used in resistant disease
reference.pathophysiology: Actinic prurigo is regarded as an immunologically mediated photodermatosis in which ultraviolet radiation, predominantly ultraviolet A, provokes a persistent T-cell driven inflammatory reaction in genetically susceptible individuals. The powerful link with specific HLA-DR4 alleles points to an antigen-presentation abnormality, and the histology and lip involvement suggest an ongoing delayed hypersensitivity response to an ultraviolet-induced cutaneous antigen. The tendency for lesions to persist on covered skin and outside the sunny season distinguishes it immunologically and clinically from ordinary polymorphic light eruption.
additionalDifferentials: Atopic eczema, especially the prurigo pattern
additionalInvestigations: Careful history for childhood onset, perennial course and characteristic cheilitis
Phototesting, which may show a reduced threshold to ultraviolet A and provocation of lesions
HLA typing, where the association with HLA-DRB1*0407 can support the diagnosis
Skin or lip biopsy, with lip histology showing follicular lymphoid hyperplasia in some cases
Antinuclear antibody testing to exclude lupus erythematosus
Porphyrin studies to exclude a cutaneous porphyria
redFlags: Disabling itch with sleep disturbance and secondary infection of excoriated lesions
Photosensitive facial rash with systemic symptoms or autoantibodies suggesting lupus
Failure to respond to standard measures, prompting reconsideration of chronic actinic dermatitis
Progressive scarring or ocular involvement requiring specialist input
reference.prognosis: Actinic prurigo tends to be chronic and can persist for many years, but it often improves gradually through adolescence and into adult life; symptom control with photoprotection, phototherapy hardening and appropriate systemic therapy is usually achievable, although complete resolution is less predictable than in polymorphic light eruption.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as ordinary polymorphic light eruption and missing the persistent, perennial and covered-site involvement
Overlooking cheilitis as a diagnostic clue, especially when it is the presenting complaint
Confusing longstanding disease in an older patient with chronic actinic dermatitis
Attributing the itch solely to atopic eczema and failing to recognise the photosensitive pattern
references: British Photodermatology Group guidance on the idiopathic photodermatoses
management: Strict photoprotection with sun avoidance, high-SPF broad-spectrum (UVA-covering) sunscreen and protective clothing
Topical corticosteroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors for cutaneous lesions and the characteristic actinic cheilitis
Thalidomide as the recognised effective systemic agent for severe or refractory disease
Prophylactic desensitising (hardening) phototherapy such as narrowband ultraviolet B before the sunny season
Emollients and antihistamines for symptomatic relief of intense pruritus
Monitoring for thalidomide-associated peripheral neuropathy and teratogenicity, with contraceptive precautions where it is used
Dermatology or photodermatology referral for phototesting and systemic therapy
